entries.name: Ancient Egyptians
entries.settlement: walled towns of the 42 nomes along the Nile; great cult capitals at Memphis and Thebes
entries.beliefs: divine king as living Horus; gods of nature and the Nile (Ra, Osiris, Isis, Horus); Ma'at order against Isfet; judgment and afterlife in the Field of Reeds
entries.fell_by: conquest by Alexander in 332 BCE, then Rome in 30 BCE; a people now embodied by the Copts
entries.notes: The Nile flood set the calendar and the tax roll; Ma'at (order) framed everything. The longest-lived civilization of antiquity.

entries.name: Naqada culture
entries.settlement: village clusters of rectangular mudbrick houses around a central hall; Hierakonpolis and Naqada grew into proto-urban centres
entries.beliefs: falcon god Horus and other animal cults; elaborate contracted burials with grave goods; afterlife for the powerful
entries.fell_by: unified into the Early Dynastic state under Narmer (c. 3100 BCE)
entries.notes: Named for the Naqada type site; the three Naqada phases (I-III) are how Egyptologists date the unification of Egypt.

entries.name: Kerma culture
entries.settlement: the round-walled city of Kerma dominated by the Western Deffufa; villages and cattle camps along the river
trade: gold, ivory, ebony and cattle out to Egypt
grain, beer and prestige goods in from Egypt
entries.beliefs: cattle cult central to ritual; great tumulus tombs of kings buried with sacrificed retainers and hundreds of cattle skulls
entries.fell_by: Egyptian conquest under Thutmose I and annexation in the early 18th Dynasty
entries.notes: The first great state south of Egypt; at its peak it rivaled the Middle Kingdom and its army threatened Upper Egypt.

entries.name: Kingdom of Kush (Napata)
entries.settlement: temple towns at Napata and Meroë; royal cemeteries at el-Kurru and Nuri
trade: iron and luxury goods in via Egypt
entries.beliefs: Amun worshipped at Jebel Barkal as a manifestation of Egyptian kingship; conservative adoption of Egyptian religion and funerary rites
entries.fell_by: Assyrian invasion (671-663 BCE) drove the Kushites from Egypt; the court withdrew south to Meroë
entries.notes: The 25th Dynasty: Nubian pharaohs (Piankhi, Taharqa) ruled a reunified Egypt and built pyramids in Sudan.

entries.name: Kingdom of Meroë
entries.settlement: ironworking cities arrayed along the Nile; royal capital at Meroë and cult centre at Musawwarat
trade: iron, gold, ivory and incense out
Roman glassware and luxuries in via Red Sea and Nile ports
entries.beliefs: Amun of Nubia plus the lion-warrior god Apedemak; royal ancestors venerated in pyramid chapels
entries.fell_by: Aksumite invasion c. 350 CE and long desertification of the Nile corridor south of the cataracts
entries.notes: More pyramids stand in Sudan than in Egypt. The Meroitic script is only partly deciphered.

entries.name: Hyksos
entries.settlement: the fortified port-capital Avaris (Tell el-Dab'a) with Levantine temples and houses
trade: Egyptian Delta by sea to Cyprus, Phoenicia and Syria
tin and copper from the east
entries.beliefs: Canaanite deities identified with Egyptian ones: Baal with Seth; their 'set(h)' cult ruled Avaris
entries.fell_by: Theban 17th Dynasty crusade; expelled by Ahmose I and pursued into Canaan (c. 1550 BCE)
entries.notes: 'Rulers of foreign lands' (heqa-khasut). They gave Egypt the horse, the chariot and the composite bow, which it then used to build an empire.

entries.name: Ptolemaic Egyptians (Macedonian dynasty)
subsistence: figs and wine on Greek-style farms
entries.settlement: Alexandria (the greatest harbour in the Mediterranean); Greek-style poleis overlaying Egyptian villages
trade: Egyptian grain out to the Mediterranean
entries.beliefs: Greek religion fused with Egyptian: the new god Serapis; twin pharaoh cult; Isis worship spread through the Greek world
entries.fell_by: Roman civil war; Cleopatra's defeat at Actium (31 BCE); annexed as a Roman province in 30 BCE
entries.notes: Greek pharaohs. Alexandria's library and lighthouse were two of the ancient world's seven wonders; the dynasty ended with Cleopatra VII.

entries.name: Copts (Egyptian Christians)
entries.settlement: villages clustered around ancient churches and desert monasteries; districts of Old Cairo (Masr al-Qadima)
entries.beliefs: Miaphysite Christianity; monasticism invented in Egypt (Anthony, Macarius, Pachomius); martyrs count in the millions under Rome and later rule
entries.notes: Direct descendants of the ancient Egyptians; the Coptic language is the last living writing of ancient Egyptian, still used liturgically.

entries.name: Medieval Islamic Egyptians
entries.settlement: Fustat replaced by Cairo (al-Qahira, 969); one of the largest cities in the world c. 1350
trade: Indian Ocean spices transshipped across the Red Sea
entries.beliefs: Sunni and (under the Fatimids) Isma'ili Shi'a Islam; Coptic Christian minority; Sufi brotherhoods pervasive
entries.fell_by: Ottoman conquest in 1517 (Marj Dabiq, Ridaniya)
entries.notes: Amr conquered Egypt in 642; Fustat then Cairo became the Arab world's metropolis and the hinge of the spice trade.

entries.name: Fatimids
entries.settlement: founded Cairo in 969 as a palace city north of Fustat; al-Azhar founded as a mosque-university
trade: monopoly on Red Sea spice transshipment
gold from West Africa via caravan
entries.beliefs: Isma'ili Shi'a Islam ruled by divine imam-caliphs; al-Azhar spread Isma'ili doctrine
entries.fell_by: Viziers seized power; Saladin abolished the caliphate in 1171 and founded the Ayyubid dynasty
entries.notes: Cairo's founders. Al-Azhar, the world's second-oldest continuously running university (970), outlived the dynasty by centuries.

entries.name: Ayyubids
entries.settlement: Cairo fortified by the Citadel; revived Damascus as a second capital
entries.beliefs: Sunni Islam, staunchly anti-Fatimid; patrons of madrasas to counter Shi'a teaching
entries.fell_by: The Mamluk coup of 1250 (Shajar al-Durr) after the French crusade of Louis IX was defeated at al-Mansura
entries.notes: Saladin's dynasty; they held Jerusalem against the Crusades and started the Citadel that still crowns Cairo.

entries.name: Mamluks
entries.settlement: Cairo, the largest city west of China c. 1400 (~400,000 people); Damascus and Aleppo as Syrian capitals
trade: monopoly on the Red Sea spice trade to Europe
entries.beliefs: Sunni Islam; sultan was protector of the Two Holy Cities; lavish endowment of mosques and madrasas
entries.fell_by: Ottoman gunpowder conquest (Marj Dabiq 1516, Ridaniya 1517)
entries.notes: Slave-soldiers bought as boys, converted, freed and promoted to sultan. They stopped the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260) and built Cairo's skyline.

entries.name: Ottoman Egyptians
entries.settlement: Cairo under Ottoman pashas and collaborating Mamluk beys; provincial towns (Rosetta, Damietta, Cairo)
trade: Red Sea coffee transshipment to Europe
entries.beliefs: Sunni (Hanafi) Islam; Sufi brotherhoods; large Christian (Coptic) and Jewish communities
entries.fell_by: Muhammad Ali's seizure of power (1805) and creation of the semi-independent khedivate
entries.notes: Three centuries of Ottoman rule: nominal imperial sovereignty, real power in the hands of Mamluk bey households.

entries.name: Modern Egyptians
entries.settlement: Cairo — one of the world's largest megacities (over 20 million in the greater area); dense Delta villages
entries.beliefs: Sunni Muslim majority (~90%); Coptic Christian minority (~10%); deep layer of pharaonic-national identity
entries.notes: Muhammad Ali modernised the army and state; the Suez Canal (1869) made Egypt the world's toll gate; 1952 revolution ended the monarchy.

entries.name: A-Group Nubians
entries.settlement: villages strung along the narrow Nile corridor; Egyptian fortresses (Buhen, Aniba) oversaw them later
trade: gold, ivory and slaves downriver to Egypt
entries.beliefs: ancestor cult; large tumulus burials for elites; absorbed Egyptian gods in late phases
entries.fell_by: absorbed and destroyed by the expanding First Dynasty Egyptian state
entries.notes: The first literate-adjacent culture of Lower Nubia; its disappearance marks Egypt's push to the Second Cataract.

entries.name: C-Group Nubians
entries.settlement: cattle-herding villages around round houses; they lived in the shadow of Egyptian border fortresses
crafts: rock art (cattle with painted hide patterns)
entries.beliefs: cattle-centered religion; burials with painted cattle skulls and round tumulus graves
entries.fell_by: Egyptian New Kingdom occupation (c. 1550 BCE); C-Group identity faded into the colonial Nubian population
entries.notes: Neighbours and occasional enemies of the Middle Kingdom forts; their cattle cults echo in Kerma and later Nubia.

entries.name: Pan-grave culture (Medjay)
entries.settlement: nomadic camps around seasonal wells; graves (pan-shaped shallow pits) are almost all that survives
crafts: distinctive shallow pan graves with cattle bucrania
entries.beliefs: warrior-nomad cult; closely related to Nubian cattle religion
entries.fell_by: absorbed into the New Kingdom military caste; 'Medjay' became simply the Egyptian word for desert police
entries.notes: The Eastern Desert nomads Egypt hired as scouts and police; later 'Medjay' meant elite paramilitary.

entries.name: Ballana / X-Group Nubians
entries.settlement: post-Meroitic Nubian kingdoms; royal courts at Ballana and Qustul
entries.beliefs: pre-Christian Nubian ancestor religion; later converted to Christianity (c. 540)
entries.fell_by: conversion to Christianity and absorption into the Nubian Christian kingdoms (Nobatia, Makuria)
entries.notes: Kings buried with sacrificed horses and silver crowns; the last pagan Nubian spectacle before Christianity.

entries.name: Christian Nubian kingdoms (Nobatia, Makuria, Alodia)
entries.settlement: cathedral cities — Dongola (Makuria), Faras, Soba (Alodia); hundreds of churches and monasteries
trade: gold and ivory south to north
entries.beliefs: Miaphysite (Coptic-aligned) Christianity; the Baqt treaty stabilized the Egyptian frontier for six centuries
entries.fell_by: gradual Islamicization after 13th-century Mamluk pressure; Alodia fell to the Funj in 1504; Makuria dissolved by 1365
entries.notes: Christian for a thousand years. Dongola withstood two Muslim sieges (642, 651) — the only Arab army turned back in Africa.

entries.name: Beja (Blemmyes)
entries.region: Eastern Desert of Egypt and Sudan
entries.settlement: nomadic camps around wells; no towns until modern times
trade: incense and ivory through the Red Sea hills
entries.beliefs: Cushitic pastoralist religion blended with Islam; ancestral shrines in the Eastern Desert mountains
entries.notes: The 'Blemmyes' who raided Roman Upper Egypt (c. 300-600 CE); the Beja still herd camels between the Nile and the Red Sea.

entries.name: Meshwesh / Libu (Libyan dynasties)
subsistence: barley and dried fish in the oases
entries.settlement: delta garrison towns (Tanis, Bubastis, Leontopolis); oasis villages (Siwa)
entries.beliefs: tribal Libyan cults fused with Egyptian ones; worshipped 'Great of Power' and the war god Sopdu/Seth
entries.fell_by: dynastic fragmentation, Nubian conquest (Shabaka, 715 BCE) and absorption into Saite Egypt
entries.notes: Libyan warriors settled as mercenaries, then took the throne as the 22nd-24th Dynasties; Shoshenq I sacked Jerusalem (c. 925 BCE).

entries.name: Sinai Bedouin
entries.settlement: nomadic camps; summer mountain pastures, winter lowland grazing; modern towns growing fast
entries.beliefs: Sunni Islam with strong tribal law (urfi); veneration of prophets' tombs (Nabi Musa etc.)
entries.notes: Tarabin, Tuwara and other tribes; guides of the ancient incense road and the Hajj caravan across Sinai.

entries.name: Funj Sultanate
entries.settlement: capital Sennar at the Blue Nile; market towns under sultan-appointed governors
trade: gum arabic and ostrich feathers out
entries.beliefs: Sufi Islam of the Arabicized Funj; the sultan claimed descent from a Umayyad prince (myth)
entries.fell_by: Muhammad Ali's Egyptian conquest of Sudan (1821)
entries.notes: An African-Arab Islamic sultanate on the Blue Nile; the Funj language died out, leaving Arabic as the tongue of Sudan.

entries.name: Nuba peoples
entries.settlement: hill villages ringed by stone walls; compounds grouped around wrestling grounds
trade: grain and cattle down to the plains
entries.beliefs: traditional mountain cults overlaid by Islam and Christianity; famous wrestling festivals (kaif) and masquerades
entries.notes: Dozens of mutually unintelligible Nuba tribes isolated by the mountains; famed for wrestling, body painting and music.

entries.name: Dinka
subsistence: sorghum and millet in the wet season
entries.settlement: dispersed homesteads across the Bahr el Ghazal and White Nile floodplains; no centralized state
trade: tribute to no one — no kings
entries.beliefs: Nhialic (the sky god) and a cattle cosmology; ox-names are a person's truest identity
entries.notes: One of Africa's largest peoples; cattle are wealth, beauty, religion and kinship all at once.

entries.name: Nuer
entries.region: Upper Nile (South Sudan and western Ethiopia)
subsistence: riverine millet and corn in the rains
entries.settlement: wet-season hamlets and dry-season camps near rivers; a segmentary lineage society with no kings or chiefs
entries.beliefs: Kwoth (God, Spirit) revealed through spirits and through cattle; prophets led migratory expansions
entries.notes: Evans-Pritchard's classic 'The Nuer' describes a stateless society of fierce egalitarianism; cattle define all social bonds.

entries.name: Shilluk
entries.settlement: riverine villages centred on the royal capital at Fashoda; the Reth (divine king) rules by descent from Nyikang
trade: grain and dried fish to the north
entries.beliefs: divine kingship — the Reth is a living embodiment of the hero Nyikang; regicide rumour when the king weakened
entries.notes: One of the world's classic divine kingships; the White Nile floodplain is their stage.

entries.name: Fayum Neolithic (Fayum A)
entries.settlement: seasonal lakeside encampments with storage pits for grain; no permanent villages yet
trade: imported grains and sheep from the Near East
entries.beliefs: unknown; burials rare and simple
entries.fell_by: climatic drying of Lake Moeris and shift to pastoral/farming sedentism (Fayum B and later)
entries.notes: The earliest farming in Egypt, contemporary with Merimde in the Delta; farming arrived as a package from the Fertile Crescent.

entries.name: Merimde culture
entries.settlement: large semi-permanent farming villages at Merimde beni Salama; oval houses in, later, rows
crafts: clay human figurines (the earliest known in Egypt)
trade: copper and ideas from the Levant
entries.beliefs: unknown; figurines suggest a household fertility/ancestor cult
entries.fell_by: declined as Faiyum and Maadi/Badarian cultures rose; Delta life re-concentrated toward the Nile branches
entries.notes: The Delta's first settled farmers; the Merimde head is among the oldest clay sculptures from Egypt.

entries.name: Tasian culture
entries.settlement: small farming hamlets along the narrow Upper Egyptian floodplain
entries.beliefs: unknown; burials with early grave goods
entries.fell_by: developed into the Badarian culture
entries.notes: The earliest named cultural horizon of Upper Egypt; Tasian pottery is its archaeological signature.

entries.name: Badarian culture
entries.settlement: small hamlets on low desert terraces above the floodplain
trade: malachite and ochre from the Eastern Desert
entries.beliefs: contracted burials on their left side, head to the south, facing west; first hints of an afterlife concern
entries.fell_by: developed into Naqada I (Amratian) with growing social complexity
entries.notes: Named for el-Badari; produced Upper Egypt's first fine pottery and its earliest known woven linen.

entries.name: Maadi culture
entries.settlement: open village at Maadi with subterranean or sunken structures; a trading community near the Wadi Digla route
trade: copper from Sinai and the Levant
entries.beliefs: unknown; cemetery at Maadi with red- ochre burials
entries.fell_by: Upper Egyptian Naqada expansion northward; absorbed into the Early Dynastic state
entries.notes: Lower Egypt's gateway for Levantine copper and ideas; the closest thing to a Lower Egyptian 'capital' before the union.

entries.name: Helwan culture
entries.region: Lower Egypt (Helwan, east of the Nile)
entries.settlement: Lower Egyptian villages around what would become Memphis; huge cemetery at Helwan (over 10,000 graves)
crafts: Early Dynastic pottery styles distinct from Upper Egypt
entries.beliefs: Early Dynastic ancestor worship; distinctive Helwan burial orientation and plastered brick-lined graves
entries.fell_by: absorbed into the Old Kingdom's unified administration (capital at Memphis)
entries.notes: The under-documented Lower Egyptian complement to Upper Egypt's Naqada; key to how unified dynastic Egypt actually worked.
